- $2^{24}$ is the size of the Class A *host* part, not a network count.

**Answer: (C)**

es_bN5Ck4GlUKlKw7vQ.q:
An Internet Service Provider (ISP) has the following chunk of CIDR-based IP addresses available with it: 245.248.128.0/20.
The ISP wants to give half of this chunk of addresses to Organization A, and a quarter to Organization B, while retaining the remaining with itself. Which of the following is a valid allocation of address to A and B?
es_bN5Ck4GlUKlKw7vQ.e:
**Key idea:** A /20 block has $2^{12}$ addresses, so half of it is a /21 and a quarter is a /22. Two rules decide whether an allocation is valid:
- Each CIDR block must start at a multiple of its own size (it must be aligned).
- The two allocations must not overlap.

245.248.128.0/20 covers third-octet values **128 – 143**, which is 16 blocks of 256 addresses.

| Size | Valid blocks (third-octet range) |
|---|---|
| Half = /21 (8 values) | 128.0/21 (128–135), 136.0/21 (136–143) |
| Quarter = /22 (4 values) | 128.0/22, 132.0/22, 136.0/22, 140.0/22 |

Checking each option:
- **(A) Valid.** A = 245.248.136.0/21 covers 136–143 and B = 245.248.128.0/22 covers 128–131. Both are aligned and they do not overlap. The ISP keeps 132.0/22 (132–135).
- **(B) Invalid.** A = 128.0/21 already contains 128.0/22, so the two allocations **overlap**.
- **(C) Invalid.** A gets a /22, which is only a quarter of the block. Also, 132.0/21 is not a legal block, because 132 is not a multiple of 8.
- **(D) Invalid.** A gets a /24, which is only 1/16 of the block, and 132.0/21 is again misaligned.

**Answer: (A)**

es_WZ7o3o22r8agF0u3.q: Let G(x) be the generator polynomial used for CRC checking. What is the condition that should be satisfied by G(x) to detect odd number of bits in error?
o: G(x) contains more than two terms
G(x) does not divide 1 + x<sup>k</sup>, for any k not exceeding the frame length
1 + x is a factor of G(x)
G(x) has an odd number of terms
es_WZ7o3o22r8agF0u3.e:
**Key idea:** Represent the bits that were flipped as an error polynomial $E(x)$. The error goes **undetected exactly when $G(x)$ divides $E(x)$**.

**Why $(1+x)$ works.** Suppose $(1+x)$ is a factor of $G(x)$.
- If $G(x)$ divided $E(x)$, then $(1+x)$ would divide $E(x)$ too, which means $E(1) = 0$ over GF(2).
- But $E(1)$ is the number of terms of $E(x)$ taken mod 2, that is, the number of flipped bits mod 2.
- For an odd number of bit errors, $E(1) = 1 \neq 0$.

So $G(x)$ can never divide such an $E(x)$, and **every odd number of bit errors is detected**.

Why the other options fail:
- **(A)** Having more than two terms is not the relevant property. For example, $1+x+x^2$ has three terms but no factor $(1+x)$. It misses the 3-bit error $E(x) = 1+x+x^2$, which $G$ divides.
- **(B)** "$G(x)$ does not divide $x^k+1$ for any $k$ up to the frame length" is the condition for detecting all **double-bit** errors, which have the form $E(x) = x^i(x^k+1)$.
- **(D)** This is the opposite of what is needed. $(1+x) \mid G(x)$ means $G(1) = 0$, so $G$ has an **even** number of terms.

**Answer: (C)**

es_lwuavs91.q:
Consider a network path P—Q—R between nodes P and R via router Q. Node P sends a file of size \({10}^6\) bytes to R via this path by splitting the file into chunks of \({10}^3\) bytes each. Node P sends these chunks one after the other without any wait time between the successive chunk transmissions. Assume that the size of extra headers added to these chunks is negligible, and that the chunk size is less than the MTU.

Each of the links P—Q and Q—R has a bandwidth of \({10}^6\) bits/sec, and negligible propagation latency. Router Q immediately transmits every packet it receives from P to R, with negligible processing and queueing delays. Router Q can simultaneously receive on link P—Q and transmit on link Q—R.

Assume P starts transmitting the chunks at time \(t=0\).

Which one of the following options gives the time (in seconds, rounded off to 3 decimal places) at which R receives all the chunks of the file?
es_lwuavs91.e:
**Key idea:** Q is a store-and-forward router that can receive and transmit at the same time, so transmission over the two links overlaps like a pipeline. The total time is the time to push all chunks onto the first link plus one extra chunk-time for the last chunk to cross the second link.

**Numbers:**
- Number of chunks: $10^6 / 10^3 = 1000$.
- Transmission time of one chunk on either link:
$$T_c = \frac{10^3 \times 8\ \text{bits}}{10^6\ \text{bits/s}} = 8\ \text{ms}$$

**Timeline:**
- P transmits chunks back-to-back. The last chunk is fully received at Q at $1000 \times 8\ \text{ms} = 8\ \text{s}$.
- Each chunk reaches Q exactly when Q finishes forwarding the previous one, so no queue builds up.
- Q then needs one more $8$ ms to send the last chunk to R.

$$T = 8 + 0.008 = 8.008\ \text{s}$$

Why the other options are wrong:
- **8.000** ignores the final hop of the last chunk.
- **16.000** would apply only if Q waited for the whole file before forwarding.

**Answer: (B)**

es_lwudz0e5.q:
Consider the entries shown below in the forwarding table of an IP router. Each entry consists of an IP prefix and the corresponding next hop router for packets whose destination IP address matches the prefix. The notation “/N” in a prefix indicates a subnet mask with the most significant N bits set to 1.

PrefixNext hop router
10.1.1.0/24R1
10.1.1.128/25R2
10.1.1.64/26R3
10.1.1.192/26R4

This router forwards 20 packets each to 5 hosts. The IP addresses of the hosts are 10.1.1.16, 10.1.1.72, 10.1.1.132, 10.1.1.191, and 10.1.1.205 . The number of packets forwarded via the next hop router R2 is _______
es_lwudz0e5.e:
**Key idea:** use longest-prefix match. Write each prefix as a range of last octets:

| Prefix | Last-octet range | Next hop |
|---|---|---|
| 10.1.1.0/24 | 0–255 | R1 |
| 10.1.1.128/25 | 128–255 | R2 |
| 10.1.1.64/26 | 64–127 | R3 |
| 10.1.1.192/26 | 192–255 | R4 |

Classify each destination by its longest matching prefix:

| Host | Matching prefixes | Longest match | Next hop |
|---|---|---|---|
| .16 | /24 | /24 | R1 |
| .72 | /24, .64/26 | /26 | R3 |
| .132 | /24, .128/25 | /25 | **R2** |
| .191 | /24, .128/25 (191 < 192) | /25 | **R2** |
| .205 | /24, .128/25, .192/26 | /26 | R4 |

Two hosts (.132 and .191) are routed through R2. Address .205 also matches the /25 entry, but the longer /26 prefix sends it to R4.

Each host receives 20 packets, so the count via R2 is
$$2 \times 20 = 40$$

**Answer: 40**

es_lwue7bez.q:
Consider sending an IP datagram of size 1420 bytes (including 20 bytes of IP header) from a sender to a receiver over a path of two links with a router between them. The first link (sender to router) has an MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) size of 542 bytes, while the second link (router to receiver) has an MTU size of 360 bytes.

The number of fragments that would be delivered at the receiver is ______________
es_lwue7bez.e:
**Key idea:** every fragment carries its own 20-byte IP header. The data in each fragment must be a multiple of 8 bytes, because the fragment offset is counted in 8-byte units; only the very last fragment of the datagram is exempt. A router fragments a datagram only when it is too big for the outgoing link, and fragments are never reassembled along the way.

Data to carry: $1420 - 20 = 1400$ bytes.

**Link 1 (MTU 542):** the largest payload is $542 - 20 = 522$. Rounding down to a multiple of 8 gives $520$.
$$1400 = 520 + 520 + 360$$
This produces **3 fragments**, with total sizes 540, 540 and 380 bytes.

**Link 2 (MTU 360):** the largest payload is $360 - 20 = 340$. Rounding down to a multiple of 8 gives $336$. All three fragments exceed 360 bytes, so the router splits each one:

| Fragment from link 1 | Data | Split on link 2 | Pieces |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 520 | 336 + 184 | 2 |
| 2 | 520 | 336 + 184 | 2 |
| 3 | 360 | 336 + 24 | 2 |

The 184-byte pieces are not the end of the datagram, so their size must be a multiple of 8; $184 = 23 \times 8$ ✓.

Fragments delivered to the receiver: $2 + 2 + 2 = 6$.

**Answer: 6**

es_lwu9ragc.q: Which of the following fields is/are modified in the IP header of a packet going out of a network address translation (NAT) device from an internal network to an external network?
es_lwu9ragc.e:
**Key idea:** for an outgoing packet, a NAT device replaces the private source address with its own public address and records the mapping in its translation table.

**(A) Source IP is modified.** The private address (for example 192.168.x.x) is replaced by the NAT's public IP. With NAPT the source port in the TCP/UDP header is also rewritten, but that field is not part of the IP header.

**(B) Destination IP is not modified.** The packet must still reach the same external host. Only the *reply* packets, coming back in, get their destination rewritten.

**(C) Header Checksum is modified.** The IPv4 header checksum covers the whole header. Changing the source address, and also the TTL decrement every router does, means it must be recomputed. The TCP/UDP checksum is updated too, because its pseudo-header includes the IP addresses.

**(D) Total Length is not modified.** NAT replaces fields of the same size, so the packet length stays the same.

**Answer: (A), (C)**

es_1kzzpg2r2.q:
Consider an enterprise network with two Ethernet segments, a web server and a firewall, connected via three routers as shown below.

What is the number of subnets inside the enterprise network?
es_1kzzpg2r2.e:
**Key idea.** A subnet is a broadcast domain bounded by layer-3 devices. Each interface of a router (here the firewall also acts as a layer-3 device) sits on its own subnet. So count every separate network segment *between* layer-3 devices, plus the LANs hanging off them.

**Reading the figure:** the firewall connects to the Internet, the left router and the top router. The top router connects to the firewall, the web server and the right router. The left and right routers each serve one Ethernet segment.

**Subnets inside the enterprise:**
1. Left Ethernet segment (left router ↔ its hosts)
2. Right Ethernet segment (right router ↔ its hosts)
3. Left router ↔ firewall link
4. Firewall ↔ top router link
5. Top router ↔ web server link
6. Top router ↔ right router link

The firewall ↔ Internet link is outside the enterprise network, so it is not counted.

Total: **6 subnets**. Answer 3 counts only the routers, and 12 or 8 count hosts or interfaces rather than segments.

**Answer: (C)**

es_40599udkwrzokdf.q:
Consider the following two statements.

S1 : Destination MAC address of an ARP reply is a broadcast address.

S2 : Destination MAC address of an ARP request is a broadcast address.

Which one of the following choices is correct?
o: S<sub>1</sub> is tue and S<sub>2</sub> is false.
Both S<sub>1</sub> and S<sub>2</sub> are false.
S<sub>1</sub> is false and S<sub>2</sub> is true.
Both S<sub>1</sub> and S<sub>2</sub> are true.
es_40599udkwrzokdf.e:
**Key idea.** The two halves of an ARP exchange are addressed differently at the MAC layer, because the sender knows different things at each step.

**S2 (ARP request → broadcast): true.** The requester knows the target's IP address but **not** its MAC address. It therefore sends the request in an Ethernet frame addressed to the broadcast MAC **FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF**, so every host on the LAN receives it. Only the host whose IP matches the target-IP field responds.

**S1 (ARP reply → broadcast): false.** The request carried the requester's own IP and MAC address (sender fields). The responder can therefore send the reply as a **unicast** frame straight to the requester's MAC address, with no need to broadcast. (A "gratuitous ARP", used to announce one's own address, is a special case and not the normal request–reply exchange.)

So S1 is false and S2 is true.

**Answer: (C)**

es_NBnmY0IAe4eR82DmWm1da9i2ynkcrohf9c.q:
Consider the following statements about the functionality of an IP based router.

I. A router does not modify the IP packets during forwarding.
II. It is not necessary for a router to implement any routing protocol.
III. A router should reassemble IP fragments if the MTU of the outgoing link is larger than the size of the incoming IP packet.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
es_NBnmY0IAe4eR82DmWm1da9i2ynkcrohf9c.e:
**Key idea:** what a router actually does to a packet it forwards.

- **I. False.** While forwarding, a router decrements the **TTL**, recomputes the **header checksum**, and may **fragment** the packet (changing total length, flags and offset). It may also rewrite options or addresses (NAT). So it does modify IP packets.
- **II. True.** A router can forward using only **static routes** configured by an administrator. Running a routing protocol (RIP, OSPF, BGP…) is not required.
- **III. False.** IP routers **never reassemble** fragments. Fragments can take different paths, so reassembly is done only by the final destination host, whatever the MTU of the next link.

Only statement II is true.

**Answer: (B)**

es_m4J8MiZFo9eAVUQ7.q: A sender uses the Stop-and-Wait ARQ protocol for reliable transmission of frames. Frames are of size 1000 bytes and the transmission rate at the sender is 80 Kbps (1Kbps = 1000 bits/second). Size of an acknowledgment is 100 bytes and the transmission rate at the receiver is 8 Kbps. The one-way propagation delay is 100 milliseconds. Assuming no frame is lost, the sender throughput is __________ bytes/second.
es_m4J8MiZFo9eAVUQ7.e:
**Key idea.** In stop-and-wait the sender delivers one frame per cycle. Here the ACK is large and goes over a slow link, so its transmission time is **not** negligible:

$$T_{\text{cycle}} = T_{\text{frame}} + T_p + T_{\text{ack}} + T_p.$$

**Frame transmission time:**

$$T_{\text{frame}} = \frac{1000 \times 8}{80\,000} = 0.1 \text{ s} = 100 \text{ ms}.$$

**ACK transmission time:**

$$T_{\text{ack}} = \frac{100 \times 8}{8\,000} = 0.1 \text{ s} = 100 \text{ ms}.$$

**Cycle time:**

$$T_{\text{cycle}} = 100 + 100 + 100 + 100 = 400 \text{ ms}.$$

**Throughput:**

$$\frac{1000 \text{ bytes}}{0.4 \text{ s}} = 2500 \text{ bytes/s}.$$

If the ACK time is ignored, the answer comes out as $1000/0.3 \approx 3333$ bytes/s, which is wrong.

**Answer: 2500**

es_VCCoOPxHC9gcTBwD.q: For a host machine that uses the token bucket algorithm for congestion control, the token bucket has a capacity of 1 megabyte and the maximum output rate is 20 megabytes per second. Tokens arrive at a rate to sustain output at a rate of 10 megabytes per second. The token bucket is currently full and the machine needs to send 12 megabytes of data. The minimum time required to transmit the data is __________ seconds.
es_VCCoOPxHC9gcTBwD.e:
**Key idea:** with a full bucket, the host can send at the peak rate $M$ until the bucket empties. Tokens keep arriving at rate $r$ during this burst. After that, output is limited to $r$.

Given: capacity $C = 1$ MB, $M = 20$ MB/s, $r = 10$ MB/s, data = 12 MB.

**Burst phase.** The bucket drains at net rate $M - r$:
$$S = \frac{C}{M-r} = \frac{1}{20-10} = 0.1\ \text{s}$$
Data sent in the burst is $M\cdot S = 20 \times 0.1 = 2$ MB (= 1 MB stored + 1 MB of new tokens).

**Steady phase.** The remaining $12 - 2 = 10$ MB goes at the token rate:
$$\frac{10}{10} = 1\ \text{s}$$

**Total:** $0.1 + 1 = 1.1$ s.

(Check: in time $t$ the bucket allows at most $C + rt = 1 + 10t$ MB, so $1 + 10t = 12$ gives $t = 1.1$ s. The peak-rate limit is respected because $20t \ge 12$.)

**Answer: 1.1**
es_VCCoOPxHC9gcTBwD.note: ExamSIDE lists 1.2, which is just 12/10 and ignores the initial burst at 20 MB/s. The correct time is 0.1 s of burst plus 1 s at the token rate, which is 1.1 s.

es_2iuNRcy4VTTJgM6r.q: Anarkali digitally signs a message and sends it to Salim. Verification of the signature by Salim requires
es_2iuNRcy4VTTJgM6r.e:
**Key idea:** the signer uses their **private** key to sign. The verifier uses the signer's **public** key to check the signature.

Anarkali signs by encrypting the message digest with *her private key*. Salim decrypts the signature with **Anarkali's public key** and compares the result with his own hash of the message. If they match, the message came from Anarkali and was not altered.

- Salim's public or private keys (B, C) play no role in verifying Anarkali's signature. They would matter only if the message were also encrypted *for* Salim.
- Anarkali's private key (D) is secret and is used only to *create* the signature.

**Answer: (A)**

es_kEWkgCGofGXSjLLc.q: Which one of the following fields of an IP header is NOT modified by a typical IP router?
es_kEWkgCGofGXSjLLc.e:
**Key idea:** A typical router (ordinary forwarding, no NAT) changes only the header fields it has to change in order to forward the datagram.

- **TTL – modified.** It is decremented at every hop.
- **Checksum – modified.** It covers the header, so the router recomputes it after changing TTL.
- **Length – can be modified.** If the datagram is larger than the next link's MTU, the router fragments it. Each fragment then gets its own total-length value (and its own offset and MF values).
- **Source address – not modified.** It identifies the original sender, and ordinary routers never change it. Only a NAT device rewrites addresses, and that is not a "typical" router.

**Answer: (B)**

es_2Kl8XMQuLr0gueqI.q:
Host A (on TCP/IPv4 network A) sends an IP datagram D to host B (also on TCP/IPv4 network B). Assume that no error occurred during the transmission of D. When D reaches B, which of the following IP header field(s) may be different from that of the original datagram D?

(i) TTL
(ii) Checksum
(iii) Fragment Offset
es_2Kl8XMQuLr0gueqI.e:
**Key idea:** Routers between network A and network B are allowed to change certain IPv4 header fields. The question asks which fields *may* differ when D reaches B.

- **(i) TTL – changes.** Every router decrements it, so the TTL that arrives at B is smaller than the one A sent.
- **(ii) Header checksum – changes.** The checksum covers the header, so each router must recompute it after changing TTL (or any other header field).
- **(iii) Fragment offset – may change.** If some network on the path has a smaller MTU, a router fragments D. Every fragment after the first then carries a non-zero offset, whereas the original D had offset 0. IPv4 reassembles fragments only at the destination, so B receives these altered headers.

All three fields can therefore differ. By contrast, ordinary routers never change the source and destination addresses.

**Answer: (D)**

es_U2leZWFhXyhZ1Oqj.q:
A sender S sends a message m to receiver R, which is digitally signed by S with its private key. In this scenario, one or more of the following security violations can take place.

I. S can launch a birthday attack to replace m with a fraudulent message.
II. A third party attacker can launch a birthday attack to replace m with a fraudulent message.
III. R can launch a birthday attack to replace m with a fraudulent message.

Which of the following are possible security violations?
es_U2leZWFhXyhZ1Oqj.e:
**Key idea:** a birthday attack finds **two** messages with the same hash. Whoever creates the colliding pair *before* signing can later swap one for the other, and the signature stays valid.

- **I. Possible.** The sender S can prepare a pair $m, m'$ with $H(m) = H(m')$ (one harmless, one fraudulent), sign $m$, and later claim the signature was on $m'$ (or swap them). The signature fits both, so S can replace $m$ with the fraudulent message.
- **II. Not possible.** A third party sees an *already signed* $m$. To replace it, they would need a different $m'$ with the same hash as this *fixed* $m$, i.e. a **second-preimage** attack. That is much harder than a birthday attack ($2^n$ vs. $2^{n/2}$ work). They also cannot get S to sign a message of their choosing.
- **III. Not possible.** The receiver R is in the same position as the third party: $m$ is fixed and signed by S, so R also needs a second preimage, not a birthday collision.

Only S can use the birthday paradox, because only S picks the message that gets signed.

**Answer: (B)**

es_jv1lTUag5ThTeFg5.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the slow start phase of the \(TCP\) congestion control algorithm. Note that \(cwnd\) stands for the \(TCP\) congestion window and \(MSS\) denotes the Maximum Segment Size.

\((i)\) \(\qquad\) The \(cwnd\) increases by \(2\) \(MSS\) on every successful acknowledgment.
\((ii)\) \(\quad\) The \(cwnd\) approximately doubles on every successful acknowledgement.
\((iii)\) \(\quad\) The \(cwnd\) increases by \(1\) \(MSS\) every round trip time.
\((iv)\) \(\quad\) The \(cwnd\) approximately doubles every round trip time.

Which one of the following is correct?
es_jv1lTUag5ThTeFg5.e:
**Key idea.** In slow start, each new ACK increases **cwnd by 1 MSS**. A window of $k$ segments produces about $k$ ACKs in one round trip, so the window goes from $k$ to $2k$: **cwnd doubles every RTT**, which is exponential growth.

Example: cwnd = 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 MSS over successive RTTs, with each ACK adding just one MSS.

**Checking each statement:**
- **(i) False.** The increase per ACK is 1 MSS, not 2 MSS.
- **(ii) False.** Doubling happens once per RTT, not on each ACK. Doubling per ACK would grow far faster than exponentially per RTT.
- **(iii) False.** An increase of 1 MSS per RTT is the **congestion avoidance** phase (additive increase), not slow start.
- **(iv) True.** Each RTT, the window roughly doubles.

Only (iv) holds.

**Answer: (C)**

es_ZXu7Lc7eOc1milET.q: Consider a long-lived \(TCP\) session with an end-to-end bandwidth of \(1\) \(Gbps\) (\(={10}^9\,\) bits-persecond). The session starts with a sequence number of \(1234.\) The minimum time (in seconds, rounded to the closest integer) before this sequence number can be used again is _______.
es_ZXu7Lc7eOc1milET.e:
**Key idea:** TCP numbers **bytes** with a 32-bit sequence number. A given sequence number can come up again only after the whole space of $2^{32}$ numbers has been used (wrap-around). At full speed, that is the time to send $2^{32}$ bytes.

Bandwidth $= 10^9$ bits/s $= 1.25\times10^{8}$ bytes/s.

$$T_{\text{wrap}} = \frac{2^{32}\ \text{bytes}}{1.25\times10^{8}\ \text{bytes/s}} = \frac{4\,294\,967\,296 \times 8}{10^{9}}\ \text{s} \approx 34.36\ \text{s}$$

So after the session starts at sequence number 1234, that number can be used again after about **34 seconds**. This is the minimum, because the link cannot send faster than 1 Gbps.

**Answer: 34 (accepted 34 to 35)**

es_Selhs3sBqCowBU0Z.q:
Consider an \(IP\) packet with a length of \(4,500\) bytes that includes a \(20\)-byte \(IPv\)\(4\) header and a \(40\)-byte \(TCP\) header. The packet is forwarded to an \(IPv4\) router that supports a Maximum Transmission Unit \((MTU)\) of \(600\) bytes. Assume that the length of the \(IP\) header in all the outgoing fragments of this packet is \(20\) bytes. Assume that the fragmentation offset value stored in the first fragment is \(0.\)

The fragmentation offset value stored in the third fragment is _______.
es_Selhs3sBqCowBU0Z.e:
**Key idea.** IP fragments everything after the IP header, and that includes the TCP header. Every fragment except the last must carry a multiple of 8 data bytes, and the offset field is counted in 8-byte units.

**IP payload to fragment:**

$$4500 - 20 = 4480 \text{ bytes (40-byte TCP header + 4440 bytes of data)}.$$

**Data per fragment:** $\text{MTU} - 20 = 600 - 20 = 580$ bytes would fit, but 580 is not a multiple of 8. Rounding down gives

$$576 \text{ bytes} \quad (576/8 = 72 \text{ units}).$$

**Offsets:**

| Fragment | Payload bytes covered | Offset (bytes/8) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 – 575 | 0 |
| 2 | 576 – 1151 | 72 |
| 3 | 1152 – 1727 | **144** |

Fragmentation continues the same way: 8 fragments in total, the last one carrying $4480 - 7 \times 576 = 448$ bytes.

**Common slips:**
- Using 580-byte fragments gives offset $1160/8 = 145$. That is not allowed, because 580 is not a multiple of 8.
- Excluding the TCP header changes nothing for the first three fragments, but it is conceptually wrong.

**Answer: 144**

es_e2i0gwOivWA6x63T.q:
Consider a simple communication system where multiple nodes are connected by a shared broadcast medium (like Ethernet or wireless). The nodes in the system use the following carrier-sense based medium access protocol. A node that receives a packet to transmit will carrier-sense the medium for \(5\) units of time. If the node does not detect any other transmission in this duration, it starts transmitting its packet in the next time unit. If the node detects another transmission, it waits until this other transmission finishes, and then begins to carrier-sense for \(5\) time units again. Once they start to transmit, nodes do not perform any collision detection and continue transmission even if a collision occurs. All transmissions last for \(20\) units of time. Assume that the transmission signal travels at the speed of \(10\) meters per unit time in the medium.

Assume that the system has two nodes \(P\) and \(Q,\) located at a distance \(d\) meters from each other. \(P\) starts transmitting a packet at time \(t=0\) after successfully completing its carrier-sense phase. Node \(Q\) has a packet to transmit at time \(t=0\) and begins to carrier-sense the medium.

The maximum distance \(d\) (in meters, rounded to the closest integer) that allows \(Q\) to successfully avoid a collision between its proposed transmission and \(P's\) ongoing transmission is _____.
es_e2i0gwOivWA6x63T.e:
**Key idea.** Q can avoid a collision only by **hearing P's signal during its own carrier-sense window**. Once that window passes quietly, Q starts transmitting (and has no collision detection). So Q is safe only if P's first bit reaches Q no later than the end of Q's sensing period.

**Timeline:**
- P starts transmitting at $t = 0$.
- Q senses the medium from $t = 0$ to $t = 5$. If it hears nothing, it transmits in the next time unit.
- P's signal travels at 10 m per time unit, so it reaches Q at $t = d/10$.

**Condition for Q to detect P in time:**

$$\frac{d}{10} \le 5 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad d \le 50 \text{ m}.$$

- If $d \le 50$: Q hears P while sensing, waits until P's 20-unit transmission ends, then senses again. No collision.
- If $d > 50$: Q's sensing window ends before P's signal arrives. Q concludes the medium is idle and transmits, and the two transmissions overlap. That is a collision.

So the maximum distance is 50 m.

**Answer: 50**

es_Oli69nzjdM7hBDFR.q: Let the size of congestion window of a TCP connection be 32 KB when a timeout occurs. The round trip time of the connection is 100 msec and the maximum segment size used is 2 KB. The time taken (in msec) by the TCP connection to get back to 32 KB congestion window is __________.
es_Oli69nzjdM7hBDFR.e:
**Key idea:** After a **timeout**, TCP sets the slow-start threshold (ssthresh) to half the current window and resets cwnd to 1 MSS. From there:
- **Slow start:** cwnd doubles every RTT until it reaches ssthresh.
- **Congestion avoidance:** cwnd then grows by 1 MSS every RTT.

Values here:
- ssthresh $= 32/2 = 16$ KB
- starting cwnd $= 1$ MSS $= 2$ KB
- RTT $= 100$ ms

| Time (ms) | cwnd (KB) | Phase |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 2 | slow start |
| 100 | 4 | |
| 200 | 8 | |
| 300 | 16 | reaches ssthresh |
| 400 | 18 | +2 KB per RTT |
| 500 | 20 | |
| 600 | 22 | |
| 700 | 24 | |
| 800 | 26 | |
| 900 | 28 | |
| 1000 | 30 | |
| 1100 | **32** | |

That is 3 RTTs of slow start (2 → 16 KB) plus $\frac{32-16}{2} = 8$ RTTs of additive increase, 11 RTTs in total:
$$11 \times 100\ \text{ms} = 1100\ \text{ms}$$

**Answer: 1100**

es_QfUe4ceLxz3ZLK37.q:
Which one of the following are used to generate a message digest by the network security protocols?
(P) RSA
(Q) SHA-1
(R) DES
(S) MD5
es_QfUe4ceLxz3ZLK37.e:
**Key idea:** a *message digest* is a fixed-length fingerprint produced by a cryptographic **hash function**. Encryption algorithms (symmetric or public-key) do not produce digests.

- **RSA (P)** – a public-key encryption / signature algorithm. It can *sign* a digest, but it does not generate one.
- **SHA-1 (Q)** – Secure Hash Algorithm, produces a 160-bit digest. ✔
- **DES (R)** – a symmetric block cipher used for encryption, not hashing.
- **MD5 (S)** – Message Digest 5, produces a 128-bit digest. ✔

So only SHA-1 and MD5 generate message digests. Options (A), (B) and (D) all include an encryption algorithm (RSA or DES), so they fail.

**Answer: (C)**

es_PAf4ACtX6Hp74SMJ.q: Which one of the following is not a client-server application?
es_PAf4ACtX6Hp74SMJ.e:
**Key idea:** A client-server application has a dedicated **server process**, listening at a well-known port, that provides a service to client processes.

**Checking each option:**
- **Internet chat:** clients connect to a chat server (for example IRC or messaging servers), which relays the messages. This is client-server.
- **Web browsing:** the browser is an HTTP client, and it talks to a web server. This is client-server.
- **E-mail:** mail user agents talk to SMTP, POP or IMAP servers, and mail servers exchange messages over SMTP. This is client-server.
- **Ping:** it is a diagnostic utility. It sends ICMP *Echo Request* messages, and the destination's **network stack (OS kernel)** replies with *Echo Reply*.
  - There is no server application, no port number, and no transport-layer connection involved.
  - Any host can ping any other host, so the roles are symmetric.
  - So ping is not a client-server application.

**Answer: (D)**

es_lwtfoe6t.q:
A user starts browsing a webpage hosted at a remote server. The browser opens a single TCP connection to fetch the entire webpage from the server. The webpage consists of a top-level index page with multiple embedded image objects. Assume that all caches (e.g., DNS cache, browser cache) are all initially empty. The following packets leave the user's computer in some order.

(i) HTTP GET request for the index page

(ii) DNS request to resolve the web server's name to its IP address

(iii) HTTP GET request for an image object

(iv) TCP SYN to open a connection to the web server

Which one of the following is the CORRECT chronological order (earliest in time to latest) of the packets leaving the computer?
es_lwtfoe6t.e:
**Key idea:** each step needs information produced by the step before it.

1. **(ii) DNS request.** The browser knows only the server's name, and every cache is empty. It cannot open a TCP connection without an IP address, so the DNS query goes out first.
2. **(iv) TCP SYN.** Once the IP is known, the browser opens the TCP connection with the three-way handshake. HTTP runs over TCP, so no HTTP request can be sent before this.
3. **(i) HTTP GET for the index page.** This is the first request on the open connection.
4. **(iii) HTTP GET for an image.** The browser learns which images exist only by parsing the index page, so these requests come after it.

The order is (ii), (iv), (i), (iii).

Why the other options fail:
- **(A)** and **(D)** send the SYN before DNS has resolved the address.
- **(B)** requests an image before the index page that refers to it.

**Answer: (C)**

es_lwu9nkto.q: TCP client P successfully establishes a connection to TCP server Q. Let \(N_P\) denote the sequence number in the SYN sent from P to Q. Let \(N_Q\) denote the acknowledgement number in the SYN ACK from Q to P. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
o: The sequence number \(N_P\) is chosen randomly by P
The sequence number \(N_P\) is always 0 for a new connection
es_lwu9nkto.e:
**Key idea:** in the three-way handshake, each side picks an **initial sequence number (ISN)**, and a SYN flag **consumes one sequence number**, just like one byte of data.

**(A) Correct.** P chooses the ISN $N_P$ (pseudo-)randomly. A random ISN means segments left over from an earlier connection on the same port pair are unlikely to fall inside the new connection's window. It also makes off-path attackers unable to guess sequence numbers to spoof or hijack the connection.

**(B) Incorrect.** The ISN is not fixed at 0. Tools such as Wireshark show *relative* sequence numbers starting at 0, but the real field holds the random ISN.

**(C) Incorrect** and **(D) Correct.** The acknowledgement number is the *next* sequence number the receiver expects. The SYN occupies sequence number $N_P$, so Q's SYN-ACK carries
$$N_Q = N_P + 1.$$
Likewise, P's final ACK will acknowledge Q's ISN plus 1.

**Answer: (A), (D)**

es_UFZoEA6rVV9x3LU1.q: Which of the following assertions is FALSE about the Internet Protocol (IP)?
o: It is possible for a computer to have multiple IP addresses
IP packets from the same source to the same destination can take different routes in the network
IP ensures that a packet is discarded if it is unable to reach its destination within a given number of hops
The packet source cannot set the route of an outgoing packets; the route is determined only by the routing tables in the routers on the way
es_UFZoEA6rVV9x3LU1.e:
**Key idea:** check each claim against how IPv4 actually behaves.

- **(A) True.** An IP address belongs to an *interface*, not to a host. A host with several interfaces (multihomed), or with virtual interfaces, has several IP addresses.
- **(B) True.** IP is a connectionless datagram service and routes every packet independently. Packets from the same source to the same destination can therefore take different paths, and can even arrive out of order.
- **(C) True.** Each router decrements the TTL field. When TTL reaches 0 the packet is discarded (and an ICMP Time Exceeded message is sent), which bounds the number of hops.
- **(D) False.** The IPv4 header has *Strict Source Route* and *Loose Source Route* options. With these, the source lists all or some of the routers the packet must traverse. So the route is not decided *only* by the routing tables along the way.

**Answer: (D)**

es_rGAHON9A43gT5VWj.q: The subnet mask for a particular network is 255.255.31.0. Which of the following pairs of IP addresses could belong to this network?
es_rGAHON9A43gT5VWj.e:
**Key idea:** two addresses are on the same network exactly when (address AND mask) gives the same result for both.

With mask 255.255.31.0:
- the first two octets must match exactly;
- the third octet is compared after ANDing it with $31 = 00011111_2$;
- the fourth octet is ignored.

- **(A)** 172.**57**.88.62 and 172.**56**.87.233: the second octets differ. ✗
- **(B)** 10.35.28.2 and 10.35.29.4: 28 AND 31 = 28, but 29 AND 31 = 29. ✗
- **(C)** 191.**203**.31.87 and 191.**234**.31.88: the second octets differ. ✗
- **(D)** 128.8.129.43 and 128.8.161.55: $129 = 10000001_2$ and $161 = 10100001_2$. ANDing each with $00011111_2$ gives 1 for both, so both lie in network 128.8.1.0. ✓

A mask with non-contiguous 1-bits like this one is unusual, but the AND rule still decides the question.

**Answer: (D)**

es_e8s51TC6RGr2vS7s.q: Which of the following functionalities must be implemented by a transport protocol over and above the network protocol?
o: Packet delivery in the correct order
es_e8s51TC6RGr2vS7s.e:
**Key idea:** "must be implemented" means a function that *every* transport protocol provides. The test is to compare TCP with UDP.

IP delivers datagrams from host to host. The transport layer's essential addition is end-to-end delivery between the communicating processes on the end systems. It does this by multiplexing and demultiplexing through port numbers.

- **(A) loss recovery, (B) duplicate detection, (C) in-order delivery:** TCP provides all three, but UDP provides none of them. They are optional services, not mandatory transport functions.
- **(D) end-to-end connectivity:** every transport protocol provides it, UDP included. It is the defining job of the layer.

**Answer: (D)**

es_lwufteny.q: Which one of the following CIDR prefixes exactly represents the range of IP addresses 10.12.2.0 to 10.12.3.255?
es_lwufteny.e:
**Key idea:** a CIDR block $/n$ contains $2^{32-n}$ addresses and must start at an address that is a multiple of its size.

**Size of the range.** 10.12.2.0 to 10.12.3.255 spans two full /24 blocks, which is $2 \times 256 = 512 = 2^9$ addresses. So the prefix length is $32 - 9 = 23$.

**Alignment.** For a /23, the lowest bit of the third octet is a host bit. The third octet here is $2 = 0000001\underline{0}_2$, whose last bit is 0. So 10.12.2.0 is a valid /23 network address.

10.12.2.0/23 therefore covers exactly 10.12.2.0 to 10.12.3.255.

Why the other options fail:
- **(B) /24** covers only 10.12.2.0 to 10.12.2.255.
- **(C) 10.12.0.0/22** covers 10.12.0.0 to 10.12.3.255, which also includes 10.12.0.x and 10.12.1.x.
- **(D) 10.12.2.0/22** is not aligned: $2$ is not a multiple of $4$ in the third octet. Its network part is really 10.12.0.0/22, which is the same overly large block as (C).

**Answer: (A)**

es_xA4Mn7xpngHbjVf0.q: One of the header fields in an IP datagram is the Time to Live (TTL) field. Which of the following statements best explains the need for this field?
o: It can be used to prioritize packets
It can be used to reduce delays
It can be used to optimize throughput
It can be used to prevent packet looping
es_xA4Mn7xpngHbjVf0.e:
**Key idea:** The TTL (Time to Live) field limits how long a datagram can stay alive in the network.

How it works:
- The sender sets TTL to an initial value, for example 64.
- **Every router that forwards the datagram decrements TTL by 1.**
- When TTL reaches 0, the router discards the datagram. It normally also sends an ICMP *Time Exceeded* message back to the source.

Why this is needed: routing tables can be temporarily inconsistent, for example during count-to-infinity in distance-vector routing or just after a link failure. A datagram can then circulate in a **routing loop**. Without TTL it would loop forever, wasting bandwidth and router buffers. TTL guarantees that every datagram dies after a bounded number of hops, so looping packets are eventually removed.

Why the other options are wrong:
- **(A)** Prioritising packets is the job of the Type-of-Service / DSCP field, not TTL.
- **(B), (C)** TTL does nothing to reduce delay or improve throughput for packets that are routed correctly. Its only effect is to remove stray packets.

(`traceroute` also makes use of TTL, but that is a side use, not the reason the field exists.)

**Answer: (D)**

es_nZHluiFJcbq5FWdi.q: Suppose computers A and B have IP addresses 10.105.1.113 and 10.105.1.91 respectively and they both use the same net mask N. Which of the values of N given below should not be used if A and B should belong to the same network?
es_nZHluiFJcbq5FWdi.e:
**Key idea:** Two hosts are on the same network exactly when `IP AND mask` gives the same network address for both.

The first three octets (10.105.1) are identical, so only the last octet matters:

$$113 = 0111\,0001_2, \qquad 91 = 0101\,1011_2$$

| Mask (last octet) | $113 \wedge \text{mask}$ | $91 \wedge \text{mask}$ | Same network? |
|---|---|---|---|
| .0 (`0000 0000`) | 0 | 0 | Yes |
| .128 (`1000 0000`) | 0 | 0 | Yes |
| .192 (`1100 0000`) | 64 | 64 | Yes |
| .224 (`1110 0000`) | **96** | **64** | **No** |

Reading the last octet from the left, the two addresses first differ in the 3rd bit (value 32): 113 has it set and 91 does not. Any mask that includes this bit puts the hosts in different networks.

Of the four options, only 255.255.255.224 does that. It places A in 10.105.1.96/27 and B in 10.105.1.64/27.

**Answer: (D)**

es_squCH770GNa0YQpW.q:
Consider a network with 6 routers R1 to R6 connected with links having weights as shown in the following diagram

All the routers use the distance vector based routing algorithm to update their routing tables. Each router starts with its routing table initialized to contain an entry for each neighbour with the weight of the respective connecting link. After all the routing tables stabilize, how many links in the network will never be used for carrying any data?
es_squCH770GNa0YQpW.e:
**Key idea:** Once distance-vector routing has converged, every router forwards along least-cost paths. A link carries data only if it lies on at least one shortest path.

In particular, a direct link is never used if its two end routers are connected more cheaply by some other route and no other shortest path passes through it.

Links: R1–R2 (6), R1–R3 (3), R2–R3 (2), R2–R4 (7), R3–R5 (9), R4–R5 (1), R4–R6 (8), R5–R6 (4).

Shortest paths:

| Pair | Shortest path | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| R1–R2 | R1–R3–R2 | 5 (direct link costs 6) |
| R1–R4 | R1–R3–R2–R4 | 12 |
| R1–R5 | R1–R3–R5 | 12 |
| R1–R6 | R1–R3–R5–R6 | 16 |
| R2–R5 | R2–R4–R5 | 8 |
| R2–R6 | R2–R4–R5–R6 | 12 |
| R3–R4 | R3–R2–R4 | 9 |
| R3–R6 | R3–R5–R6 | 13 |
| R4–R6 | R4–R5–R6 | 5 (direct link costs 8) |

All remaining pairs are neighbours and use their direct link.

- **R1–R2 (cost 6):** R1→R3→R2 costs only 5, so this link is never chosen.
- **R4–R6 (cost 8):** R4→R5→R6 costs only 5, so this link is never chosen.
- **Every other link** lies on at least one shortest path. For example, R3–R5 is used by R1→R5 (12, against 13 via R2–R4) and by R3→R6, and R2–R4 is used by R1→R4.

No two paths tie, so exactly **2 links** are never used.

**Answer: (C)**

es_xtimgMI1wyxTnc1F.q:
Consider a network with 6 routers R1 to R6 connected with links having weights as shown in the following diagram

Suppose the weights of all unused links in the previous question are changed to 2 and the distance vector algorithm is used again until all routing tables stabilize. How many links will now remain unused?
es_xtimgMI1wyxTnc1F.e:
**Key idea:** Once distance-vector routing stabilises, every router uses shortest paths. A link is "unused" if it lies on **no** shortest path between any pair of routers.

**Step 1: unused links with the original weights.**
- **R1–R2 (6):** the path R1→R3→R2 costs $3+2 = 5 < 6$, so this link is unused.
- **R4–R6 (8):** the path R4→R5→R6 costs $1+4 = 5 < 8$, so this link is unused.
- **R2–R4 (7):** it is the cheapest way from R2 to R4 (the alternative R2→R3→R5→R4 costs 12), so it is used.
- **R3–R5 (9):** it beats R3→R2→R4→R5, which costs 10, so it is used.

**Step 2: set R1–R2 = 2 and R4–R6 = 2, then re-check every link.**

| Link | Direct cost | Best alternative | Used? |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1–R2 | 2 | R1→R3→R2 = 5 | yes |
| R1–R3 | 3 | R1→R2→R3 = 4 | yes |
| R2–R3 | 2 | R2→R1→R3 = 5 | yes |
| R2–R4 | 7 | R2→R3→R5→R4 = 12 | yes |
| R3–R5 | 9 | R3→R2→R4→R5 = 10 | yes |
| R4–R5 | 1 | R4→R6→R5 = 6 | yes |
| R4–R6 | 2 | R4→R5→R6 = 5 | yes |
| R5–R6 | 4 | R5→R4→R6 = **3** | **no** |

**Why R5–R6 is never used.** Any path that crosses R5–R6 can swap that hop for R5→R4→R6. That swap costs 3 instead of 4, so the path gets strictly cheaper. Hence no shortest path ever uses R5–R6.

Exactly **one** link remains unused.

**Answer: (B)**
es_xtimgMI1wyxTnc1F.note: ExamSIDE lists (A) 0. After R1–R2 and R4–R6 become 2, the path R5→R4→R6 costs 3, which is less than 4, so link R5–R6 is never on a shortest path and exactly one link stays unused.

es_r0Amg6H03kp6aZQW.q: A link has a transmission speed of 10<sup>6</sup> bits/sec. It uses data packets of size 1000 bytes each. Assume that the acknowledgement has negligible transmission delay, and that its propagation delay is the same as the data propagation delay. Also assume that the processing delays at the nodes are negligible. The efficiency of the stop-and-wait protocol in this setup is exactly 25%. The value of the one-way propagation delay (in milliseconds) is ___________.
es_r0Amg6H03kp6aZQW.e:
**Key idea.** Stop-and-wait sends one packet per cycle of $T_t + 2T_p$, where the ACK's transmission time and the processing delays are negligible. Its efficiency is

$$\eta = \frac{T_t}{T_t + 2T_p}.$$

**Transmission time:**

$$T_t = \frac{1000 \times 8 \text{ bits}}{10^6 \text{ bits/s}} = 8 \text{ ms}.$$

**Use $\eta = 0.25$:**

$$\frac{8}{8 + 2T_p} = \frac14 \;\Longrightarrow\; 8 + 2T_p = 32 \;\Longrightarrow\; 2T_p = 24 \;\Longrightarrow\; T_p = 12 \text{ ms}.$$

**Check:** the cycle is $8 + 24 = 32$ ms, and the sender transmits for 8 of those ms, which is 25%.

**Answer: 12**

es_Foll2rdzIoGPrsdq.q: Two hosts are connected via a packet switch with 10<sup>7</sup> bits per second links. Each link has a propagation delay of 20 microseconds. The switch begins forwarding a packet 35 microseconds after it receives the same. If 10000 bits of data are to be transmitted between the two hosts using a packet size of 5000 bits, the time elapsed between the transmission of the first bit of data and the reception of the last bit of the data in microseconds is _________.
es_Foll2rdzIoGPrsdq.e:
**Key idea:** store-and-forward switching with pipelining. The switch must receive a whole packet, waits 35 µs, then retransmits it. Meanwhile the host is already sending the next packet.

- Transmission time per packet: $T_t = \dfrac{5000}{10^7}\text{ s} = 500\ \mu s$
- Propagation per link: $T_p = 20\ \mu s$. Switch processing delay: $35\ \mu s$. Number of packets: $10000/5000 = 2$.

**Packet 1:**
- Host sends 0–500; last bit reaches the switch at 520.
- Switch starts forwarding at 555 and finishes transmitting at 1055.

**Packet 2:**
- Host sends 500–1000; last bit reaches the switch at 1020.
- It could be forwarded at 1055, which is exactly when the switch's output link becomes free.
- Switch transmits 1055–1555; the last bit reaches the destination at $1555+20 = 1575\ \mu s$.

Equivalently: $T = 2T_t + T_p + 35 + T_t + T_p = 1000+20+35+500+20 = 1575$.

**Answer: 1575**

es_gNV5fNwyQcICh5Ex.q: Host A sends a UDP datagram containing 8880 bytes of user data to host B over an Ethernet LAN. Ethernet frames may carry data up to 1500 bytes (i.e. MTU = 1500 bytes). Size of UDP header is 8 bytes and size of IP heard is 20 bytes.There is no option field in IP header How many total number of IP fragments will be transmitted and what will be the contents of offset field in the last fragment?
es_gNV5fNwyQcICh5Ex.e:
**Key idea.** IP fragments the **IP payload**, which here is the UDP header plus the user data. Every fragment except the last must carry a multiple of 8 data bytes, and the fragment offset field counts in **8-byte units**.

**IP payload size:**

$$8880 + 8 \text{ (UDP header)} = 8888 \text{ bytes}.$$

**Maximum data per fragment:** MTU − IP header $= 1500 - 20 = 1480$ bytes. This is already a multiple of 8 ($1480/8 = 185$).

**Number of fragments:**

$$\left\lceil \frac{8888}{1480} \right\rceil = \lceil 6.005 \rceil = 7.$$

Six fragments carry $6 \times 1480 = 8880$ bytes, and the 7th carries the remaining 8 bytes.

**Offset of the last fragment:** it starts at byte 8880 of the payload, so

$$\text{offset} = \frac{8880}{8} = 1110.$$

**Why the other options fail:**
- "6 fragments" forgets the 8-byte UDP header, which is also part of the IP payload.
- 8880 gives the offset in bytes, but the field stores it in 8-byte units.

**Answer: (C)**

es_935LRZUDqiJJCRtZ.q:
Consider the following routing table at an IP router:

For each IP address in Group I identify the correct choice of the next hop from Group II using the entries from the routing table above.
o: i - a, ii - c, iii - e, iv - d
i - a, ii - d, iii - b, iv - e
i - b, ii - c, iii - d, iv - e
i - b, ii - c, iii - e, iv - d
es_935LRZUDqiJJCRtZ.e:
**Key idea.** The router uses **longest prefix match**. For each destination, AND the address with each entry's mask, check whether the result equals that network number, and among the matches pick the one with the longest mask. Only the third octet matters here, because the first two octets (128.96) are the same everywhere.

The routing table, as address ranges:

| Entry | Prefix | Third-octet range | Next hop |
|---|---|---|---|
| 128.96.170.0 | /23 (mask 254) | 170–171 | Interface 0 |
| 128.96.168.0 | /23 | 168–169 | Interface 1 |
| 128.96.166.0 | /23 | 166–167 | R2 |
| 128.96.164.0 | /22 (mask 252) | 164–167 | R3 |
| 0.0.0.0 | /0 | everything | R4 |

**Matching each address:**
- **(i) 128.96.171.92:** $171 \,\&\, 254 = 170$, which matches 170.0/23 → **Interface 0 (a)**.
- **(ii) 128.96.167.151:** $167 \,\&\, 254 = 166$ matches 166.0/23 (R2), and $167 \,\&\, 252 = 164$ also matches 164.0/22 (R3). The longer prefix (/23) wins → **R2 (c)**.
- **(iii) 128.96.163.151:** $163 \,\&\, 254 = 162$ matches no /23 entry, and $163 \,\&\, 252 = 160 \ne 164$. Only the default route matches → **R4 (e)**.
- **(iv) 128.96.165.121:** $165 \,\&\, 254 = 164$ matches no /23 entry, but $165 \,\&\, 252 = 164$ matches 164.0/22 → **R3 (d)**.

That gives i–a, ii–c, iii–e, iv–d. Options (C) and (D) send (i) to Interface 1, and (B) sends (ii) to R3, which ignores longest-prefix matching.

**Answer: (A)**

es_m80a3jxd.q:
A machine receives an IPv4 datagram. The protocol field of the IPv4 header has the protocol number of a protocol X .

Which ONE of the following is NOT a possible candidate for X ?
es_m80a3jxd.e:
**Key idea:** the IPv4 *Protocol* field names the protocol whose message sits **directly** inside the IP payload. A protocol that runs on top of UDP or TCP is never named there; the field would say UDP (17) or TCP (6) instead.

- **ICMP:** carried directly in IP, protocol number **1**. Possible.
- **IGMP:** carried directly in IP, protocol number **2**. Possible.
- **OSPF:** runs directly over IP, with no TCP or UDP, using protocol number **89**. Possible.
- **RIP:** an application-level protocol carried in **UDP** on port 520. The IP Protocol field of a RIP packet therefore holds 17 (UDP), and RIP has no IP protocol number of its own. **Not possible.**

**Answer: (D)**

es_m80a3x0i.q: Consider a network that uses Ethernet and IPv4. Assume that IPv4 headers do not use any options field. Each Ethernet frame can carry a maximum of 1500 bytes in its data field. A UDP segment is transmitted. The payload (data) in the UDP segment is 7488 bytes. Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment including IPv4 header?
es_m80a3x0i.e:
**Key idea:** IP fragments the *whole UDP segment*, which is the UDP header plus data. Each fragment adds its own 20-byte IP header. Every fragment except the last must carry a multiple of 8 data bytes.

**IP payload to carry:** the UDP data plus the 8-byte UDP header,
$$7488 + 8 = 7496 \text{ bytes}$$

**Maximum data per fragment:** the Ethernet data field is 1500 bytes, so
$$1500 - 20 = 1480 \text{ bytes}$$
This is already a multiple of 8, since $1480 = 185 \times 8$.

**Fragments:**
$$7496 = 5 \times 1480 + 96$$
This gives 5 full fragments of $1480 + 20 = 1500$ bytes each, plus a last fragment carrying 96 bytes of data.

**Last fragment size:** $96 + 20 = 116$ bytes. The total is $5 + 1 = 6$ fragments.

Why the other options are wrong:
- **(B), 88 bytes:** forgets the UDP header, giving $7488 - 7400 = 88$ data bytes, and also omits the IP header.
- **(C), 108 bytes:** forgets the UDP header but adds the IP header, $88 + 20$.

**Answer: (D)**

es_lwufcfq6.q:
Node X has a TCP connection open to node Y. The packets from X to Y go through an intermediate IP router R. Ethernet switch S is the first switch on the network path between X and R. Consider a packet sent from X to Y over this connection.

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the destination IP and MAC addresses on this packet at the time it leaves X?
o: The destination IP address is the IP address of R
The destination IP address is the IP address of Y
The destination MAC address is the MAC address of S
The destination MAC address is the MAC address of Y
es_lwufcfq6.e:
**Key idea:** IP addresses are end-to-end, while MAC addresses are hop-by-hop. A MAC address names the next *layer-3* hop on the local link.

**Destination IP address.** X addresses the datagram to the final destination Y. Router R only forwards it and never appears as the destination IP. So (B) is true and (A) is false.

**Destination MAC address.** Y is on another network, beyond router R. X finds that the next hop is its gateway R, gets R's MAC address with ARP, and puts R's MAC in the Ethernet frame.
- **(C) is false.** An Ethernet switch is transparent at layer 2. It forwards frames by their destination MAC and is not the addressee of the frame. A switch port typically has no MAC address that hosts send frames to.
- **(D) is false.** Y's MAC is not visible from X's LAN. When R forwards the packet, it builds a new frame for the next link.

So the packet leaves X with destination IP $= $ Y and destination MAC $= $ R. Only (B) is among the options.

**Answer: (B)**

es_lwufgekh.q: Which of the following statements about IPv4 fragmentation is/are TRUE?
o: The fragmentation of an IP datagram is performed only at the source of the datagram
The fragmentation of an IP datagram is performed at any IP router which finds that the size of the datagram to be transmitted exceeds the MTU
The reassembly of fragments is performed only at the destination of the datagram
The reassembly of fragments is performed at all intermediate routers along the path from the source to the destination
es_lwufgekh.e:
**Key idea:** in IPv4, *fragmentation* can happen at any hop, but *reassembly* happens only at the final destination.

- **(A) False.** The source host may fragment, but so can any IPv4 router. (Restricting fragmentation to the source is the IPv6 rule.)
- **(B) True.** If a router must forward a datagram onto a link whose MTU is smaller than the datagram, it fragments it, provided the DF (Don't Fragment) bit is not set. If DF is set, the router drops the datagram and sends an ICMP "fragmentation needed" message instead.
- **(C) True.** Fragments of one datagram may take different paths and may be fragmented again later on. Only the destination host reassembles them, using the Identification, Fragment Offset and MF fields.
- **(D) False.** Routers do not reassemble fragments. Doing so would require buffering every fragment, and the fragments might not even all pass through the same router.

**Answer: (B), (C)**

es_lwuflt2j.q: Which of the following fields of an IP header is/are always modified by any router before it forwards the IP packet?
es_lwuflt2j.e:
**Key idea:** a router that forwards a packet must decrement its TTL, and any change to the header means the header checksum has to be recomputed.

- **(A) Source IP: not always modified.** An ordinary router leaves both addresses alone. Only special middleboxes such as NAT devices rewrite the source address, and the question asks about *any* router.
- **(B) Protocol: not modified.** This field names the payload protocol (TCP = 6, UDP = 17, ICMP = 1, …), and the payload does not change in transit.
- **(C) TTL: always modified.** Every router decrements TTL by 1 to stop packets circulating forever. When TTL reaches 0, the router drops the packet and sends an ICMP Time Exceeded message.
- **(D) Header Checksum: always modified.** The IPv4 checksum covers the whole header, including TTL. Since TTL changes at every hop, the checksum must be recomputed or incrementally updated at every hop.

(Fields such as Total Length, Flags and Fragment Offset change only when the router fragments the packet.)

**Answer: (C), (D)**

es_DFWW6kyVFzogCIL0.q: The distance between two stations M and N is L kilometers. All frames are K bits long. The propagation delay per kilometer is t seconds. Let R bits/second be the channel capacity. Assuming that processing delay is negligible, the minimum number of bits for the sequence number field in a frame for maximum utilization, when the sliding window protocol is used, is:
es_DFWW6kyVFzogCIL0.e:
**Key idea:** for maximum utilization, the sender must keep transmitting until the ACK for its first frame arrives. The window $W$ must therefore cover one frame's transmission time plus the round-trip propagation time, and the sequence-number field needs enough bits to number $W$ frames.

- Transmission time: $T_t = \dfrac{K}{R}$.
- One-way propagation delay: $T_p = Lt$.
- Window needed:
$$W = \frac{T_t + 2T_p}{T_t} = 1 + \frac{2LtR}{K} = \frac{2LtR + K}{K}.$$
- Sequence-number bits: $n = \left\lceil \log_2 \dfrac{2LtR + K}{K} \right\rceil$.

Why the other options fail:
- (A) counts the transmission time twice: $(2LtR + 2K)/K$.
- (B) leaves out the frame's own transmission time.
- (D) is half of what is needed.

**Answer: (C)**

es_STFpO80Y6JXF9cc8.q: The address of a class B host is to be split into subnets with a 6-bit subnet number. What is the maximum number of subnets and the maximum number of hosts in each subnet?
es_STFpO80Y6JXF9cc8.e:
**Key idea:** a class B address has 16 host bits. Taking 6 of them for the subnet number leaves $16-6=10$ bits for hosts.

- **Hosts per subnet:** the all-0s host (network address) and the all-1s host (broadcast) are reserved, so there are $2^{10}-2 = 1022$ usable hosts.
- **Subnets:** $2^6 = 64$ patterns. Classical subnetting (RFC 950) also excluded the all-0s and all-1s subnet numbers, which leaves $64 - 2 = 62$.

Checking the options:
- (A) and (B): 262142 hosts would need 18 host bits, which leaves no room for a 6-bit subnet.
- (D): 1024 forgets to subtract the network and broadcast addresses.
- (C): 62 subnets and 1022 hosts is the only consistent choice. It follows the classical convention, under which both counts exclude their all-0s and all-1s patterns.

**Answer: (C)**

es_9VQSGeopw67VPBgX.q: Which one of the following uses UDP as the transport protocol?
es_9VQSGeopw67VPBgX.e:
**Key idea:** applications that need a reliable byte stream use TCP. Short request/response exchanges, where the application can simply resend a lost message, use UDP.

- **HTTP:** TCP (port 80); web pages and objects must arrive complete and in order.
- **Telnet:** TCP (port 23); an interactive session that needs reliability.
- **DNS:** **UDP (port 53)** for ordinary queries. A single small query and a single small reply don't justify a TCP handshake, and the resolver simply retries on a timeout. TCP is used only for zone transfers or replies too large for UDP.
- **SMTP:** TCP (port 25); mail must be delivered reliably.

**Answer: (C)**

es_qxlv6jaUYCILj1qv.q:
Match the following:

List - I

(P) SMTP
(Q) BGP
(R) TCP
(S) PPP

List - II

(1) Application layer
(2) Transport layer
(3) Data link layer
(4) Network layer
(5) Physical layer
es_qxlv6jaUYCILj1qv.e:
**Key idea:** Place each protocol in the layer whose function it performs.

- **(P) SMTP → (1) Application layer.** It transfers e-mail between mail servers, and it runs on top of TCP (port 25).
- **(Q) BGP → (4) Network layer.** It is the inter-domain (inter-AS) **routing** protocol. Routing is a network-layer function, even though BGP messages are carried over TCP.
- **(R) TCP → (2) Transport layer.** It provides reliable, connection-oriented end-to-end delivery between processes.
- **(S) PPP → (3) Data link layer.** It handles framing and link control over a point-to-point serial link.

That gives P-1, Q-4, R-2, S-3.

**Why the other options fail:**
- (C) puts PPP at the physical layer. PPP defines framing, not signalling.
- (A) and (D) put SMTP at the transport layer, and TCP at the data link or application layer.

**Answer: (B)**

es_mmz0yrh4.q: With respect to a TCP connection between a client and a server, which one of the following statements is true?
o: The client and server use a two-way handshake mechanism before the start of data transmission.
The server cannot initiate closing of the connection before the client initiates closing of the connection.
The client and server can initiate closing of the connection at the same time.
es_mmz0yrh4.e:
- **(A) False.** TCP sets up a connection with a **three-way** handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. A two-way handshake could not reliably agree on both sides' initial sequence numbers.
- **(B) False.** The two endpoints are symmetric when it comes to closing. Either one, client or server, may send the first FIN; this is called an active close. For example, an HTTP server often closes first.
- **(C) False.** TCP is **full-duplex**: data flows both ways at once on the same connection, and each direction has its own sequence numbers.
- **(D) True.** TCP supports a **simultaneous close**. Both sides can send FIN at the same time. Each side then goes FIN_WAIT_1 → CLOSING → TIME_WAIT, acknowledging the other's FIN, and the connection closes cleanly.

**Answer: (D)**

es_m7wyc1q3.q: Consider the 3-way handshaking protocol for TCP connection establishment. Let the three packets exchanged during the connection establishment be denoted as P1, P2 and P3, in order. Which of the following option(s) is/are TRUE with respect to TCP header flags that are set in the packets?
es_m7wyc1q3.e:
**Key idea:** in the three-way handshake each side sends one SYN, carrying its own initial sequence number, and each side acknowledges the other's SYN.

| Packet | Direction | SYN | ACK | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | client → server | 1 | 0 | client's SYN with ISN $x$ |
| P2 | server → client | 1 | 1 | server's SYN with ISN $y$, and ack $= x+1$ |
| P3 | client → server | 0 | 1 | ack $= y+1$, connection established |

Checking each option:
- **(A) False.** P3 is a pure ACK. Its SYN flag is 0, because the client has already sent its SYN in P1.
- **(B) True.** P2 is the SYN-ACK, so both flags are set.
- **(C) False.** P2 must have SYN = 1, since this is how the server sends its own ISN.
- **(D) True.** P1 is the initial SYN.

**Answer: (B), (D)**

es_1lfeybb6y.q: Suppose two hosts are connected by a point-to-point link and they are configured to use Stop-end-Wait protocol for reliable data transfer. Identify in which one of the following scenarios, the utilization of the link is the lowest.
o: Longer link length and lower transmission rate
Longer link length and higher transmission rate
Shorter link length and lower transmission rate
Shorter link length and higher transmission rate
es_1lfeybb6y.e:
**Key idea:** for Stop-and-Wait, with transmission time $T_t$ and one-way propagation delay $T_p$, the utilisation is
$$U = \frac{T_t}{T_t + 2T_p} = \frac{1}{1+2a}, \qquad a = \frac{T_p}{T_t}$$

Utilisation is **lowest when $a$ is largest**, which means a large $T_p$ and a small $T_t$:
- A **longer link** increases $T_p$, since $T_p = \text{length}/\text{signal speed}$.
- A **higher transmission rate** decreases $T_t$, since $T_t = \text{frame size}/\text{rate}$.

Both changes in (B) increase $a$. The sender pushes the frame out quickly and then sits idle through a long round trip.

Why the other options give higher utilisation:
- **(A):** a lower rate makes $T_t$ larger, which partly hides the long delay.
- **(C):** a short link with a slow rate gives the smallest $a$, so this is the *highest* utilisation.
- **(D):** a short link keeps $T_p$, and therefore $a$, small.

**Answer: (B)**

es_35ivwjQeIOMIkS2S3N7km5fk050o8gc.e:
**Key idea.** Powers of 3 modulo 5 repeat in a cycle. By Fermat's little theorem, $3^{4} \equiv 1 \pmod 5$ because 5 is prime and $\gcd(3,5)=1$, so the exponent can be reduced modulo 4.

**The cycle:**

$$3^1 \equiv 3,\quad 3^2 = 9 \equiv 4,\quad 3^3 = 27 \equiv 2,\quad 3^4 = 81 \equiv 1 \pmod 5.$$

**Reduce the exponent:**

$$51 = 4 \times 12 + 3 \;\Longrightarrow\; 3^{51} = (3^4)^{12} \cdot 3^3 \equiv 1^{12} \cdot 27 \equiv 27 \pmod 5.$$

$$27 \bmod 5 = 2.$$

**Check another way:** $3 \equiv -2 \pmod 5$, so $3^2 \equiv 4 \equiv -1$. Then $3^{51} = (3^2)^{25}\cdot 3 \equiv (-1)^{25} \cdot 3 = -3 \equiv 2 \pmod 5$.

**Answer: 2**

es_hQ1kd7mGE6lH0iL0.q: Suppose that everyone in a group of N people wants to communicate secretly with the N - 1 others using symmetric key cryptographic system. The communication between any two persons should not be decodable by the others in the group. The number of keys required in the system as a whole to satisfy the confidentiality requirement is
es_hQ1kd7mGE6lH0iL0.e:
**Key idea:** in symmetric-key cryptography both parties share the same secret key. For the conversation between two people to be unreadable by anyone else, **every pair needs its own key**.

The number of distinct pairs among $N$ people is

$$\binom{N}{2}=\frac{N(N-1)}{2}.$$

The key used by A and B is the same in both directions (A→B and B→A), so there is no need to double the count. That rules out $N(N-1)$ in (B). $2N$ in (A) would be the count for public-key cryptography (one public/private pair per person), and $(N-1)^2$ in (D) has no meaning here.

**Answer: (C)**

es_m7wyc1a7.q:
A packet with the destination IP address 145.36.109.70 arrives at a router whose routing table is shown. Which interface will the packet be forwarded to?

Subnet Address Subnet Mask
(in CIDR notation)		 Interface
145.36.0.0 /16 E1
145.36.128.0 /17 E2
145.36.64.0 /18 E3
145.36.255.0 /24 E4
Default \(-\) E5
es_m7wyc1a7.e:
**Key idea:** apply longest-prefix match. For each entry, AND the destination with the mask and compare the result with the subnet address.

Destination: 145.36.109.70. The third octet is $109 = 01101101_2$.

| Entry | Mask on 3rd octet | $109 \wedge \text{mask}$ | Subnet's 3rd octet | Match? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 145.36.0.0/16 | 0 | 0 | 0 | ✓ |
| 145.36.128.0/17 | 128 ($10000000_2$) | 0 | 128 | ✗ |
| 145.36.64.0/18 | 192 ($11000000_2$) | 64 | 64 | ✓ |
| 145.36.255.0/24 | 255 | 109 | 255 | ✗ |

The /18 block 145.36.64.0 covers third-octet values 64 to 127, and 109 falls inside it.

The /16 and /18 entries both match. The longer prefix, /18, wins, so the packet goes to **E3**. E1 would be used only if nothing more specific matched. E5 (default) is not needed because specific entries match.

**Answer: (A)**

es_7znX1nEboNvENnaK.q:
Consider a network with five nodes, N1 to N5, as shown below.

The network uses a Distance Vector Routing protocol. Once the routes have stabilized, the distance vectors at different nodes are as following

N1 : ( 0, 1, 7, 8, 4 )
N2 : ( 1, 0, 6, 7, 3 )
N3 : ( 7, 6, 0, 2, 6 )
N4 : ( 8, 7, 2, 0, 4 )
N5 : ( 4, 3, 6, 4, 0 )

Each distance vector is the distance of the best known path at that instance to nodes, N1 to N5, where the distance to itself is 0. Also, all links are symmetric and the cost is identical in both directions. In each round, all nodes exchange their distance vectors with their respective neighbors. Then all nodes update their distance vectors. In between two rounds, any change in cost of a link will cause the two incident nodes to change only that entry in their distance vectors

The cost of link N2 - N3 reduces to 2 in (both directions). After the next round of updates, what will be the new distance vector at node, N3?
es_7znX1nEboNvENnaK.e:
**Key idea:** In one round of distance-vector routing, each node recomputes every entry from its neighbours' vectors **as they were before the round**:
$$D_x(y) = \min_{v}\{c(x,v) + D_v(y)\}$$

Links (from the figure): N1–N2 = 1, N2–N5 = 3, N2–N3 = 6, N3–N4 = 2, N4–N5 = 4.

**Before the round.** The cost of N2–N3 drops to 2, and only that entry changes at the two end nodes:
- N2 becomes $(1, 0, \mathbf{2}, 7, 3)$
- N3 becomes $(7, \mathbf{2}, 0, 2, 6)$
- N4 is unchanged at $(8, 7, 2, 0, 4)$

**N3's update.** N3 has two neighbours, N2 (cost 2) and N4 (cost 2):

| Dest | via N2: $2 + D_{N2}$ | via N4: $2 + D_{N4}$ | New |
|---|---|---|---|
| N1 | 2 + 1 = **3** | 2 + 8 = 10 | 3 |
| N2 | 2 + 0 = **2** | 2 + 7 = 9 | 2 |
| N3 | — | — | 0 |
| N4 | 2 + 7 = 9 | 2 + 0 = **2** | 2 |
| N5 | 2 + 3 = **5** | 2 + 4 = 6 | 5 |

So N3's new vector is $(3, 2, 0, 2, 5)$.

Why the other options fail:
- **(B) and (D)** keep the cost to N5 at 6, missing the cheaper route $2 + 3$ through N2.
- **(C) and (D)** keep the cost to N1 at 7, missing the route $2 + 1$ through N2.

**Answer: (A)**

es_cnmq0jGTVF09oz1kvzjf76htyjzvzi46s.q: Which of the following protocol pairs can be used to send and retrieve e-mails (in that order)?
es_cnmq0jGTVF09oz1kvzjf76htyjzvzi46s.e:
**Key idea.** Sending mail is a *push*: the client hands mail to its server, and the server relays it to the recipient's server. **SMTP** does this. Retrieving mail is a *pull*: the recipient's user agent fetches mail from its mailbox server, using **POP3** or **IMAP**.

**Checking the ordered pairs (send, retrieve):**
- **(A) IMAP, SMTP:** reversed. IMAP retrieves mail and SMTP sends it.
- **(B) SMTP, POP3:** SMTP sends and POP3 retrieves. Correct.
- **(C) IMAP, POP3:** both are retrieval protocols, so neither can send.
- **(D) SMTP, MIME:** MIME is not a transfer protocol at all. It is an encoding standard for non-ASCII content and attachments inside the message body.

**Answer: (B)**

es_TvXvMxSU3wSt3gGiZr7kejek2756f4c.q: In an RSA cryptosystem, the value of the public modulus parameter n is 3007. If it is also known that \(\varphi\)(n) = 2880, where \(\varphi\)() denotes Euler's Totient Function, then the prime factor of n which is greater than 50 is ______.
es_TvXvMxSU3wSt3gGiZr7kejek2756f4c.e:
**Key idea:** in RSA, $n = pq$ and $\varphi(n) = (p-1)(q-1) = n - (p+q) + 1$. From $n$ and $\varphi(n)$ we can get the sum and the product of $p$ and $q$, then solve a quadratic.

$$p + q = n - \varphi(n) + 1 = 3007 - 2880 + 1 = 128$$
$$pq = 3007$$

So $p, q$ are the roots of $t^2 - 128t + 3007 = 0$:

$$t = \frac{128 \pm \sqrt{128^2 - 4\cdot3007}}{2} = \frac{128 \pm \sqrt{16384 - 12028}}{2} = \frac{128 \pm \sqrt{4356}}{2} = \frac{128 \pm 66}{2}$$

This gives $t = 97$ or $t = 31$. Check: $31 \times 97 = 3007$ ✔ and $30 \times 96 = 2880$ ✔.

The prime factor greater than 50 is 97.

**Answer: 97**

es_FRHW11bt03QzswKYdm7kejek27iphgr.q: Consider that 15 machines need to be connected in a LAN using 8-port Ethernet switches. Assume that these switches do not have any separate uplink ports. The minimum number of switches needed is _____.
es_FRHW11bt03QzswKYdm7kejek27iphgr.e:
**Key idea.** The switches have no dedicated uplink ports, so connecting two switches uses up one ordinary port on each. To connect $k$ switches into one LAN you need at least $k-1$ inter-switch links, as in a tree or chain, which take $2(k-1)$ ports.

**Ports left for machines with $k$ switches:**

$$8k - 2(k-1) = 6k + 2.$$

**Smallest $k$ with $6k + 2 \ge 15$:**
- $k = 1$: 8 ports, not enough.
- $k = 2$: $6(2) + 2 = 14$ ports, one short. Each switch spends a port on the link between them, leaving $7 + 7 = 14$.
- $k = 3$: $6(3) + 2 = 20$ ports, enough. For example, chain S1–S2–S3: S1 and S3 each have 7 free ports and S2 has 6, for 20 in total.

So at least 3 switches are needed.

**Answer: 3**

es_mmz0z9xy.q: An ISP having an address block 202.16.0.0/15 assigns a block of 6000 IP addresses to a client, using the classless internet domain routing (CIDR) super-netting approach. Which of the following address blocks can be assigned by the ISP?
es_mmz0z9xy.e:
**Key idea:** a CIDR block must have a power-of-two size and be *aligned*, meaning its start address is a multiple of its size. It must also lie inside the ISP's block.

**Block size needed:** $2^{12} = 4096 < 6000 \le 8192 = 2^{13}$, so 13 host bits, which is a **/19** block.

**ISP block:** 202.16.0.0/15 covers 202.16.0.0 to 202.17.255.255. The second octet may be 16 or 17.

**Alignment of a /19:** the prefix uses 16 bits plus the top 3 bits of the third octet. So the third octet must be a multiple of $2^5 = 32$: 0, 32, 64, 96, …, 224. The fourth octet must be 0.

| Option | Second octet | Third octet | Multiple of 32? | Valid? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (A) 202.16.0.0/19 | 16 | 0 | yes | ✓ |
| (B) 202.17.64.0/19 | 17 | 64 | yes | ✓ |
| (C) 202.16.32.0/19 | 16 | 32 | yes | ✓ |
| (D) 202.17.24.0/19 | 17 | 24 | no ($24 = 00011000_2$, so host bits are set) | ✗ |

Option (D) is not a valid /19 network address. The /19 that contains 202.17.24.0 actually starts at 202.17.0.0.

**Answer: (A), (B), (C)**

es_m7wyc123.q: Suppose a message of size 15000 bytes is transmitted from a source to a destination using IPv4 protocol via two routers as shown in the figure. Each router has a defined maximum transmission unit (MTU) as shown in the figure, including IP header. The number of fragments that will be delivered to the destination is _________ . (Answer in integer)
es_m7wyc123.e:
**Key idea:** IPv4 fragmentation happens at each router whose outgoing MTU is too small. Every fragment except the last must carry a payload that is a multiple of 8 bytes. Fragments are **not reassembled** at intermediate routers, so already-fragmented pieces may be fragmented again. IP header = 20 bytes.

**Router-1 (MTU 5000):** maximum payload $= 5000 - 20 = 4980$, rounded down to a multiple of 8 gives **4976**.
The 15000 data bytes split into $4976 + 4976 + 4976 + 72$, which is **4 fragments**.

**Router-2 (MTU 3000):** maximum payload $= 3000 - 20 = 2980$, rounded down to a multiple of 8 gives **2976**.
- Each 4976-byte fragment becomes $2976 + 2000$, i.e. 2 fragments. For three such fragments that is 6.
- The 72-byte fragment fits as is: 1 fragment.

Total delivered to the destination $= 6 + 1 = 7$.

(If the 15000 bytes are taken to include a 20-byte header, the data is 14980, which splits as $4976\times3 + 52$. The count is still 7.)

**Answer: 7**

es_b5AGaNqB7K2FFTVX.q: Consider a CSMA/CD network that transmits data at a rate of 100 Mbps (10<sup>8</sup> bits second) over a 1 km(kilometer) cable with no repeaters. If the minimum frame size required for this network is 1250 bytes, what is the signal speed (km/sec) in the cable?
es_b5AGaNqB7K2FFTVX.e:
**Key idea.** In CSMA/CD the sender has to still be transmitting when news of a collision comes back from the far end of the cable. That takes up to one round trip, so the minimum frame satisfies

$$T_t = 2T_p \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L_{\min} = 2 \cdot T_p \cdot B.$$

**Transmission time of the minimum frame:**

$$T_t = \frac{1250 \times 8}{10^8} = \frac{10^4}{10^8} = 10^{-4} \text{ s} = 100 \;\mu\text{s}.$$

**Propagation delay:**

$$T_p = \frac{T_t}{2} = 50 \;\mu\text{s}.$$

**Signal speed:**

$$v = \frac{d}{T_p} = \frac{1 \text{ km}}{50 \times 10^{-6} \text{ s}} = 20\,000 \text{ km/s}.$$

The other options come from leaving out the factor 2 (10000 km/s) or from other arithmetic slips.

**Answer: (D)**

es_0t6eLnHSRrUggz1D.q: Consider a network connected two systems located 8000 kilometers apart. The bandwidth of the network is 500 × 10<sup>6</sup> bits per second. The propagation speed of the media is 4 × 10<sup>6</sup> meters per second. It is needed to design a Go-Back-N sliding window protocol for this network. The average packet size is 10<sup>7</sup> bits. The network is to be used to its full capacity. Assume that processing delays at nodes are negligible. Then the minimum size in bits of the sequence number field has to be ___________.
es_0t6eLnHSRrUggz1D.e:
**Key idea.** To use the link at full capacity, the sender must keep transmitting until the first ACK returns. The window therefore has to cover one full cycle, $W \ge \dfrac{T_t + 2T_p}{T_t} = 1 + 2a$. In Go-Back-N with an $n$-bit sequence number, the window can be at most $2^n - 1$.

**Delays:**

$$T_p = \frac{8000 \times 10^3 \text{ m}}{4 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}} = 2 \text{ s}, \qquad T_t = \frac{10^7 \text{ bits}}{500 \times 10^6 \text{ bits/s}} = 0.02 \text{ s}.$$

**Required window:**

$$a = \frac{T_p}{T_t} = \frac{2}{0.02} = 100, \qquad W = 1 + 2a = 201 \text{ packets}.$$

**Sequence-number bits:** we need $2^n - 1 \ge 201$, i.e. $2^n \ge 202$.
- $n = 7$ gives $2^7 = 128$, which is too small.
- $n = 8$ gives $2^8 = 256$, which is enough.

So the sequence number field needs at least 8 bits.

**Answer: 8**

es_40599uckwrzo0pm.q:

es_BAKCzTGuJGx4vumE.q: Consider a 128 × 10<sup>3</sup> bits/second satellite communication link with one way propagation delay of 150 milliseconds. Selective retransmission (repeat) protocol is used on this link to send data with a frame size of 1 kilobyte. Neglect the transmission time of acknowledgement. The minimum number of bits required for the sequence number field to achieve 100% utilization is _________.
es_BAKCzTGuJGx4vumE.e:
**Key idea.** To reach 100% utilization, the sender must keep transmitting for one whole round trip, which requires a window of $W \ge \dfrac{T_t + 2T_p}{T_t}$ frames. In Selective Repeat the sender and receiver windows are equal, and each can be at most **half** the sequence space: $W \le 2^{n-1}$.

**Transmission time** (1 KB = 1024 bytes = 8192 bits):

$$T_t = \frac{8192}{128 \times 10^3} = 0.064 \text{ s} = 64 \text{ ms}.$$

**Required window:**

$$W \ge \frac{64 + 2 \times 150}{64} = \frac{364}{64} \approx 5.69 \;\Rightarrow\; W = 6 \text{ frames}.$$

Taking 1 KB = 1000 bytes gives $T_t = 62.5$ ms and $W \ge 362.5/62.5 = 5.8$, which still rounds up to 6.

**Sequence-number bits:** Selective Repeat needs at least $2W = 12$ distinct sequence numbers.
- $n = 3$ gives $2^3 = 8 < 12$, too few.
- $n = 4$ gives $2^4 = 16 \ge 12$, enough.

The answer is not 3 because 3 bits would suffice for Go-Back-N ($2^3 - 1 = 7 \ge 6$), but Selective Repeat needs twice the window size.

**Answer: 4**

es_z9e6dDRS8IhLDLty.q: A bit-stuffing based framing protocol uses an 8-bit delimiter pattern of 01111110. If the output bit-string after stuffing is 01111100101, then the input bit-string is
es_z9e6dDRS8IhLDLty.e:
**Key idea:** The flag $01111110$ contains six consecutive 1s. To keep that pattern from appearing inside the data:
- the sender **inserts a 0 after every five consecutive 1s**;
- the receiver undoes this by **deleting the 0 that follows any five consecutive 1s**.

De-stuffing the output `01111100101`:

```
0 1 1 1 1 1 [0] 0 1 0 1
  ^^^^^^^^^  ^
  five 1s    stuffed 0 -> removed
```

Removing the stuffed bit leaves
$$0\,11111\,0101 = 0111110101$$

**Check by re-stuffing.** In `0111110101` the run of five 1s gets a 0 inserted after it: `011111` + `0` + `0101` = `01111100101`, which matches the given output.

Why the other options fail:
- **(A)** `0111110100` re-stuffs to `01111100100`, whose last bit differs from the output.
- **(C), (D)** contain six or more consecutive 1s, which would have forced a stuffed 0 at a different position.

**Answer: (B)**

es_VsdjYpLNL9PBCVIR.q: A network has a data transmission bandwidth of 20 × 10<sup>6</sup> bits per second. It uses CSMA/CD in the MAC layer. The maximum signal propagation time from one node to another node is 40 microseconds. The minimum size of a frame in the network is __________ bytes.
es_VsdjYpLNL9PBCVIR.e:
**Key idea.** For CSMA/CD to detect a collision reliably, a station must still be transmitting when the collision signal gets back from the farthest node. In the worst case this takes a full round trip, $2T_p$, so

$$T_t \ge 2T_p \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L_{\min} = 2\,T_p \times B.$$

**Compute:**

$$L_{\min} = 2 \times (40 \times 10^{-6} \text{ s}) \times (20 \times 10^{6} \text{ bits/s}) = 1600 \text{ bits}.$$

$$\frac{1600}{8} = 200 \text{ bytes}.$$

(Using $T_p$ instead of $2T_p$ would give 100 bytes. That isn't enough, because a collision near the far end would only be reported after the sender had already finished transmitting.)

**Answer: 200**

es_IfVTllEpDFlRADDc.q:
For the IEEE 802.11 MAC protocol for wireless communication, which of the following statements is/are TRUE?


I. At least three non-overlapping channels are available for transmissions.
II. The RTS-CTS mechanism is used for collision detection.
III. Unicast frames are ACKed.
es_IfVTllEpDFlRADDc.e:
**Key idea:** the main features of IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) MAC: CSMA/**CA**, link-layer ACKs and the channel plan.

- **I. True.** In the 2.4 GHz band, 802.11b/g has 11 channels (in the US), and channels **1, 6 and 11** do not overlap. The 5 GHz band has many more. So at least three non-overlapping channels are available.
- **II. False.** Wireless stations cannot reliably detect collisions (hidden terminals, own signal swamps reception). RTS/CTS reserves the channel to **avoid** collisions (CSMA/CA). It does not detect them.
